The feature was unreachable by the only role authorized to use it - the third time today that a slice shipped its records and its screens without a door. An administrator now has a list of every placement, marked with who supervises it or that nobody does, and an Internships entry in the admin navigation. It carries the same reach administrable_by? grants: the placement record, never a weekly report.

The page went from 404 to 403 without anybody deploying it. Every path on the documentation host now answers with a Vercel Security Checkpoint - the maintenance page, the roadmap, the dashboard root - where the root had answered 200 the same afternoon. That is bot protection or attack-challenge mode on the host, not the failed build this item chased for three days, and a real browser driven headless gets Failed to verify your browser, Code 21. So bin/rails error_pages:published now tells a challenge apart from a missing page and names the host setting rather than sending the reader to the deploy log, and RB-0006 gained the escalation: a maintenance page a visitor has to pass a challenge to read is not a maintenance page. The host question is the Platform Owner's, and it is now the whole of what OPS-001 waits on. It is also wider than this item - while the challenge is on, the development dashboard is unreadable to anyone the project shares it with.

The user asked for the menubar to become a dropdown menu. The header had carried the destinations twice: a horizontal rail above 1180px and a burger panel below it, with a test whose job was to prove the two agreed. They are now one list in one dropdown at every width, so a destination sits in the same place on a phone and on a desk and adding one cannot quietly overflow a rail that had run out of room - which it nearly had, at nine entries for a student after today's Internships addition. The panel and its Stimulus controller already existed and were reused unchanged, so the change is mostly subtraction: the rail markup is gone, the panel carries the nav landmark and its label rather than being a second one, and the button gained a visible Menu label from the sm breakpoint up because a lone burger on a wide header reads as an afterthought rather than as the way in. The nav: breakpoint stays - the admin two-column screens fold there - but its comment no longer claims the header reads it. Two system walks clicked a nav link directly and now open the menu first through a navigate_to helper, which is the honest cost of the change: reaching a destination is two clicks rather than one. The user then moved it after the brand icon and asked for categories. The button now sits immediately after the shield, where the mark and the way into the app read as one gesture and the rail on the right stays what it is - preferences, notifications, and the account; the panel opens left-aligned under it. app_nav_groups replaces app_nav_items as the source, with app_nav_items kept as its flattening so every check that a nav entry is a door its workspace can open still reads one list and grouping can reorder destinations without adding or dropping one. A learner reads Learn, Track, and Beyond the course; an instructor Teaching and University; an administrator Administration and University; a company member Your company and Students. The headings match how the footer already sorts the same screens. Moving the control left also shortened the keyboard path to it: it is the third tab stop from the top now - skip link, brand, menu - where it had been at the end of the utility rail, and Enter opens it, Tab walks into the panel, Escape closes it and returns focus to the button. Then the categories themselves became the menubar, which is where this ends up: Learn, Track and Beyond the course sit after the brand, each its own dropdown, rather than three headings inside one panel. Each category is a separate dropdown controller, which is what makes opening one close the others - a click on another button is outside the first, and closeOnOutsideClick already handled that with no shared state. The category holding the current screen is marked on the bar, so the section is legible without opening anything. Two things came out of driving it rather than testing it. The bar had overflow-x-auto so it could scroll when tight, and a scrolling row is a clipping container: the panels opened and were invisible, clipped by the bar they hung from. And three category buttons plus the utility rail do not fit a phone at all. So the bar never scrolls, and below md it becomes one button carrying every category as a heading - two renderings again, but both read app_nav_groups and a shared item partial, so they cannot disagree about what exists or how the current page is marked, only about how many buttons carry it.

ADR-0041 decision 5, and the finding that reframed it: the platform was never document-free. CandidateProfile has accepted a resume and portfolio files since SPEC-0029, under a content-type allowlist, a ten-megabyte ceiling, candidate-owned export, and a delete that removes attachments before the row. So the question was not what a document contract should say - most of it was already written - but what internship records may attach and what that contract did not cover: scanning, a retention clock, and post-internship access. The user answered all four questions. A request shares the resume rather than storing one: resume_shared_at is a timestamp, not a blob, because a second copy would mean two retention clocks and two deletions for the one document the platform is least entitled to duplicate, and it would break the promise that deleting a resume from a profile deletes it everywhere - which a test now pins. A deliverable is a new record because the work a student produces during a placement had no home anywhere. The safety envelope is SPEC-0029's, reused rather than reinvented, and nothing is scanned - which is exactly why the other half matters more: this is the first path in the application by which one person reads a file another person uploaded, so every download is served by an app route as an attachment under nosniff, with the content type re-identified by Active Storage rather than trusted from the uploader, and never through a signed blob URL, because a signed URL authorizes the link rather than the reader and outlives both the placement and the membership that justified it. Access ends with its record: a company reads a shared resume while the request is open and while the internship it produced runs, never after a rejection or completion, and reads deliverables only while the placement is open. The faculty supervisor was offered a reader's seat and the user declined it - the assignment grants the placement and its weekly reports, not the student's files. The student deletes their own work and nothing expires on a timer. Two things came out of building it rather than specifying it: the model's transition! leaves a record dirty on status after it syncs, so a plain update! for the sharing stamp was refused by the guard that catches untracked status changes - it uses update_columns now, the same idiom acknowledgement already used - and opening the screen showed the request notice still promising no resume or file uploads, which the same page now disproved. That copy is corrected in both locales, and the two places the ADR and spec still said text only are marked superseded rather than quietly edited.

bin/rails test:spec[SPEC-0041] reads a lifecycle document's enforced_by and runs exactly those files, so the rule recorded this morning is a command rather than a copy-paste from a doc. It works on decision records too, names the system tests instead of running them because they are the slow half that belongs to the gate, and refuses with a useful message when a spec lists nothing - an empty enforced_by is the actual bug, and the fix is to fill it in rather than to run everything. It shells out rather than calling Rake::Task[test].invoke: the Rails test task takes its files from the command line, so invoking it in process quietly ran all 1,204 tests, which is the one thing the task exists to avoid. Alongside it, the two dead ends the route sweep found are closed. A dismissed job recommendation can be brought back: the undo action had existed since job discovery shipped with nothing linking to it, so a misclick hid a recommendation permanently for anyone who did not know the route. And the company internship-applications index is gone rather than linked - it had no template at all, so an authorized reader would have met a missing-template error, while the program's own screen already lists its applications with the decide and evaluate controls on them. The one test that used that route to prove cross-organization refusal now proves it through the accept action, which is the stronger assertion.

The company internship-applications index removed earlier today was one instance of a class: a route that exists, resolves, and is a 500 waiting for its first authorized visitor, because the action has no template and nothing links to it. test/operations/route_reachability_test.rb closes the class. It asserts every route resolves to an action that exists, and that every GET either renders a template or appears in WITHOUT_TEMPLATE with a sentence saying why - nine do today, all of them send_data or a partial, each now named. Writing it was a lesson in the repo's own rule that a test must fail for the intended reason before it is trusted: the first version passed against a deliberately planted template-less route, because it decided an action was safe by reading forty lines from the method definition and swept up a render from the next method down. The second version read only the method's own body and then produced two false positives - policies#privacy and #terms are endless methods delegating to a private show that renders, and both answer 200. Source-sniffing cannot decide this, so the heuristic is gone: a template-less GET is now a written exception rather than a guess, which is also the version that fails loudly when the next one appears. Both defect shapes were planted and confirmed failing before the test was kept. Registered in the agent-flow invariant table and in the CLAUDE.md invariant list, because a rule not written as a test does not exist.

bundler-audit went red on a run that had passed an hour earlier, and nothing in this repository had changed to cause it: the ruby-advisory-db refreshed at 02:25 with two new entries. CVE-2026-66066 is arbitrary file read and remote code execution in Active Storage variant processing, against activestorage 8.1.3; CVE-2026-71847 is a use-after-free in JSON::ResumableParser on truncated duplicate-key streams, against json 2.21.1. Rails is now 8.1.3.1 and json 2.21.2, both the versions the advisories name, taken conservatively so nothing else moved. The application builds no variants anywhere - a grep finds no .variant call - so the exposure was narrower than the title suggests, but the repository treats a security scan as a gate rather than as advice and the fix is a patch release. Worth noting for its own sake: this is the second time today the timing mattered more than the content. A gate is only as good as the day it last ran, and this one would have blocked the build for anyone who pulled main tomorrow morning without touching a line of it.

SPEC-0041 ships four increments and a fresh database showed none of them: no request to decide, no placement to advance, no week to acknowledge, no supervisor, no file. Every screen built over the last two days was an empty state, which is the one thing a demo cannot demonstrate. The seeds now walk one internship the whole way - a student's request, a shared resume, the company's approval, an active placement, a weekly report, an administrator-assigned supervisor, and a deliverable - through the real APIs rather than written straight into the tables, so the seeded rows are the ones the app itself would produce, guards and all. The replant caught the ordering error immediately: sharing a resume is only allowed while a request is open, and the first version shared it after approval. It had passed in development because the flag was already set there by hand, which is exactly the kind of thing a wiped database is for. Two replants in a row produce the same single set of rows.

A defect introduced this morning by INT-006 and caught by measuring rather than by reading: the placement screen filtered deliverables with a per-record readable_by?, and the company half of that rule is two membership lookups, so the screen cost two queries per file. Measured at seven queries for one deliverable and fifteen for five - it grew with the pile, which is exactly what test/models/query_budget_test.rb and the agent-flow invariant table already forbid for a cohort. InternshipPlacement#deliverables_readable_by asks the company question once and returns a scope: the whole list for a decider while the placement is open, and the author's own otherwise, which is the same rule readable_by? states for one record. The budget test now covers it, and the regression was planted and confirmed failing at seven versus twenty-five queries before the fix was kept. Seeding the internship exposed a second, older trap the repository had already documented in test/fixtures/organizations.yml: a table the seeds write and the fixtures do not name is never cleared between them, so a seeded row outlives the users it points at and the next fixture load dies on a foreign key. Eight tables needed the same deliberately-empty file - the five internship tables, candidate profiles, and both Active Storage tables - and the note in each says why it is empty.

The roadmap and the backlog disagreed in both directions at once, and nothing read both files. The UTCC summary table still called five finished milestones Next or Later, and the consolidated table still described the Student Internship Request Platform as increments 1 to 3 after increment 4 had shipped. The roadmap is what a person opens to decide what to build next, so a stale cell sends somebody to build what already exists or to leave alone what nobody has started. script/validate-backlog, already a gate through bin/docs, now reads docs/roadmap.md as well: a milestone the backlog tracks is Complete on the roadmap exactly when every one of its items is complete, checked in the consolidated table, the summary table, and each milestone section status line. Milestones with no backlog items — the M0 baseline and the unaccepted proposals M12, M13, M14 — have nothing to compare and are left alone.

Ecosystem M13 is order 3 in the unified plan and had no ADR and no specification, so the roadmap gate had nothing to confirm or refuse. Writing them turned up why: the proposal intake it proposes to extend has no governing document either, and three of its four statuses are unreachable. Nothing in app/ assigns status, there is no index or review screen, and the author-facing page renders a status that can never change. M13's stated outcome is the proportion of proposals receiving an auditable decision and an author-visible explanation; that proportion is zero by construction, so the baseline the roadmap defers to discovery is already known. ADR-0049 is proposed, not accepted: record the existing boundary first, make the first increment triage rather than participation, keep the audience as it is, and keep the explanation in-app because ADR-0004 still defers production email. SPEC-0049 is a draft record of the shipped intake, naming the dead statuses as a defect rather than a design. No code changed and no M13 delivery item exists.

Writing SPEC-0049 showed that the proposal intake's two refusals were the two things no test touched: one contributor reading another's proposal, and an incomplete submission re-rendering the form. Each is one line of controller, which is exactly how they get lost. Both hold, and are now asserted along with a staff account being turned away from the form. That third test is where the draft specification turned out to be wrong: a signed-in account with the wrong role is redirected to root with the forbidden flash, not refused outright, because Authorization#authorize_role lands both of its denials there. The specification now says so. The one gap left open is deliberate: that no code path changes status cannot be usefully asserted until ADR-0049 decision 6 settles the status vocabulary, since either form of the assertion would be deleted by the change that answers it.

bin/docs warned about 28 documents past review_by on every run, which is how a warning stops being read. Most of it was not debt: 19 are accepted documents past a mechanical created-plus-seven stamp, and 4 are correctly draft because their work is genuinely blocked - ADR-0010 and SPEC-0010 for UTCC SSO, ADR-0022 and SPEC-0022 for production deployment, which the backlog already records as M6-002 and M9-004. The real finding was 4 documents whose frontmatter contradicted their own bodies. M7-001 and M7-002 shipped on 2026-08-03 with the approval recorded in this file in the user's own words, their specs carry enforced_by lists pointing at tests that exist and pass, and their review-state blockquotes say the user approved them - while status still said draft, and the README index said draft too, so nothing could catch it. ADR-0012, ADR-0013, SPEC-0012, and SPEC-0013 now record the acceptance that happened, with the date it was recorded kept distinct from the date it was given. SPEC-0015 was deliberately left as draft: its work is complete and its tests pass too, but its own text says it remains blocked on the unreviewed supported-flag rows, scopes, runtime consumers, and academic policy, so any rule that swept it up with the others would have been wrong.

bin/docs printed 28 identical review_by lines on every run, and reading 28 identical lines is how DOCS-014's finding stayed hidden: four documents whose work had shipped nine days earlier, sitting in the same undifferentiated list as nineteen accepted documents a week past a mechanical stamp. The two are now counted and phrased apart. A draft or proposed document past its review date is stalled and names its owners, because it is waiting on a person. Anything else past its date is due for re-review, because it is waiting on the calendar. Neither aborts the build; a decision nobody has made yet is a fact about the project, not a broken gate. The output went from 28 undifferentiated warnings to 5 stalled and 19 due for re-review, and the 5 are a clean cross-check on the backlog: ADR-0010 and SPEC-0010 are M6-002, ADR-0022 and SPEC-0022 are M9-004, and SPEC-0015 is the feature-flag specification deliberately left draft by DOCS-014. Run before today's flip it would have listed 9, and the 4 extra would have been the ones nobody had noticed.

A timestamp in the future is how this file stops being a record and starts being a plan, and it was introduced here by hand today: writing several entries in one sitting and spacing them half an hour apart to keep them ordered walked DEV-006, DOCS-014, and DEV-007 past the clock, so each claimed to be finished before it was. Those three are corrected to 10:25, 10:45, and 11:00, and the top-level updated_at with them. The ordering instinct was right and the method was wrong: updates is not sorted and does not need to be, so an entry never has to be dated later than the one above it. script/validate-backlog now warns on any item or update timestamp in the future and errors on one that will not parse at all. It warns rather than aborts because 19 timestamps across 8 items from earlier sessions are still ahead of the clock, by an hour for DEV-002 through OPS-002 and by up to twenty for INT-005, OPS-001, and UX-007. Whether those clocks were wrong or the entries were deliberately post-dated is for whoever wrote them; the check asks on every run instead of nobody asking.

Recorded a diagnosis, not a fix. Chasing the /maintenance 404 after a push showed the whole documentation site is frozen: it serves a backlog stamped 2026-08-07T22:51:23 and a build stamp of commit 37b6250d, a 2026-08-08 merge into agent/recruitment-platform-vertical-slices. Probing by document age gives a clean cutoff - everything created on or before 2026-08-07 serves 200, everything after it 404s, including all of M11-SIR and both documents written today. The cause is two separate failures on the hosting side. GitHub Actions is locked for billing, so every pages.yml run fails in nine seconds without starting a step, and one earlier run titled 'fix: unbreak the dashboard deploy' failed the same way while looking like a code problem. Vercel is building a branch that is not main. The repository builds clean at 293748f through every gate the deploy runs. Two consequences worth carrying: this item cannot be fixed from the codebase, and every evidence_url in this file currently resolves to nothing, because script/validate-backlog checks that a URL looks like a rendered page and never fetches it.

Diagnosing OPS-001 showed this file's evidence links had been resolving to nothing since 2026-08-07 with no check noticing, because the check read their shape and stopped: a URL ending in .html passed whether or not any document stood behind it. Fetching them would tie the build to a deploy it does not control, which is the wrong trade. The half that is ours is checkable offline - the site is built from docs/, so specs/spec-x.html is a promise that docs/spec-x.md exists, and validate-markdown-graph already holds every Markdown link to exactly that rule. Backlog evidence was the one link surface without it, on both evidence[].url and evidence_url. All 122 relative links resolve today, so a passing run proved nothing and the rule was tested against injected breakage instead: two invented links, one on an item and one on an update, both caught by name. This is a guard rather than a repair. It does nothing for the outage - those links still resolve to nothing in practice until the GitHub billing lock clears - but the next bad link now fails at the gate instead of silently, which is the same reasoning as the route reachability invariant: close the class, not the instance.

An audit of app/services found the one real defect it produced. ADR-0037 suppresses application totals and status cells below five, and its fitness function says counts below the threshold are suppressed consistently; the code decided it on the total alone, so once the total cleared five every per-status cell published its exact count. Six applications, five submitted and one screening, produced a cell of one and named the single person who had reached screening to a reader who can see who applied - while the line under the table told them populations below five were suppressed. Suppressing the cell alone would have hidden nothing, because five published beside a total of six returns the sixth by subtraction, so the total is withheld whenever any cell is. Zero is still published: a cell of zero names nobody and hiding it would redact six of seven statuses. All four existing tests passed unmodified, which is the better evidence that this restored the recorded intent rather than bending it.

ADR-0048 records that four counts run on each page load. Measured, the work surface cost 20 queries when application figures were suppressed and 27 when they were not: the four are the dashboard's own, and underneath them OrganizationReporting counted once per status across vocabularies of six and seven while postings asked each relation twice. Thirteen now, on both paths, by grouping the counts - every number on the board survived, so the ADR's prescribed remedy of caching does not apply either. Nothing had guarded this screen; the query budget covered the instructor report, the roster, the catalog, standings and deliverables and stopped there. The new ceiling was measured rather than guessed, by forcing the assertion to fail once to read the true number.

JobAlertNotifier and Observability::Instrumentation had no test anywhere. The first decides whether a student hears about new matches and how often, so the rule that stops a daily alert firing twice - a lock, a re-read of alerts_due? inside it, and a timestamp written only when a notification was created - was resting on nothing. The second is three global subscribers installed from an initializer, and untested a subscriber is a particular risk: it fails by going quiet, and a silent failure detector reads exactly like a healthy system. Thirteen tests, all passing on the first run; neither service was broken, both were unasserted. One asserts install is idempotent, because a second subscription would report every incident twice, and another passes a password in a payload and asserts it never reaches the emitted signal.

REAL_TOPIC_KEYS and TOPIC_GRADING both list the twelve real topics and are linked by a fetch that raises, so a topic added to one and not the other is a KeyError found by the first learner who opens it. An empty check list is worse: it grades every submission as a pass, because an empty array is all-true, and then divides by zero working out the score, so the learner is credited and immediately shown a 500. The guard for that divisor exists three method definitions away on the default grading path and not on the real-topic one. That asymmetry is deliberately left alone - whether a topic with no checks should pass, fail, or refuse to grade is a decision about grading and belongs to whoever owns the curriculum - but the table should never reach that state, and being a frozen constant it can only get there in a code change. Four invariants now fail there instead, including that every recorded solution passes its own topic's checks, which would otherwise let the course present an answer it marks wrong.

The repository states the English and Thai locale files must stay in sync and nothing checked it. Discipline had held - 2426 keys each, no difference in either direction - but this was the second stated invariant of the week being kept by hand rather than by a gate, and the first had already drifted by the time anybody looked. The failure does not announce itself: Rails is configured with fallbacks to English, so a key missing from Thai neither raises nor renders a translation-missing marker. It renders English to a reader who chose Thai, on a page that looks like it worked, and Thai is the default locale. Three checks, reading the two files rather than the I18n backend because the backend also carries the framework's English defaults. One empty Thai key was injected to confirm two of the three fire before the file was restored.

ADR-0048 decision 7 said an inactive organization is not reachable, the same way its other screens are not. The second clause was untrue when written: the work surface and the reporting page both refused a suspended company, while /company/:slug served a member its record normally, so the screen the decision was about was the strictest of the three rather than one of a set. The record refuses a member now. Administrators are a deliberate exception and a load-bearing one - /admin lists only active organizations and every membership action redirects back to this page, so refusing them too would let somebody suspend a company and leave no screen anywhere that could manage it. Decision 7 is amended rather than rewritten, keeping the original sentence with the correction underneath. This came out of an audit finding that was first reported backwards and withdrawn; reading the caller to withdraw it is what turned up that visible_to? has no status check at all.

The user accepted ADR-0049 on 2026-08-12, the day it was proposed, so Ecosystem M13 now has a boundary rather than a nine-hundred-line description. Five of roadmap section 15's twelve product decisions are settled: registered-only intake for the first increment, evolve the existing proposal_requests rather than replace it, a triage-only lifecycle with recorded transitions, human-recorded references to the roadmap and backlog rather than generated ones, and a baseline of zero that is measurable today rather than deferred to discovery. Seven remain open and no work may assume an answer to them - field visibility, voting, comments and moderation, role mapping, the private security-report path, search and attachments and notifications, and AI data use. Two consequences worth separating. Decision 1 is authorized immediately and is documentation only: SPEC-0049 records the shipped intake, and the ADR's own fitness function is not satisfied until that specification is accepted rather than draft. Increment 1 - a triage screen, a decision record, an author-visible reason, and the status vocabulary settled with its check constraint so no status exists that the code cannot reach - is authorized in scope but not scheduled. Accepting a boundary is not a delivery commitment, and M13 stays Proposed on the roadmap until a backlog item and the roadmap gate carry it into execution.

The user accepted SPEC-0049 on 2026-08-12, which satisfies ADR-0049 decision 1 and closes the gap that had blocked any change to proposals: the intake shipped without an ADR or a specification, so there was no recorded statement of who may submit, what is stored, who may read it, or what happens next, and nothing to keep consistent with. The confirmation the document was waiting on was specifically invariant 4, that three of the four statuses cannot be reached and the author-facing page displays one of them as though it were live. Accepting the specification settles what the boundary is, not that all of it is desirable - the defect is now recorded rather than unknown, and ADR-0049 decision 6 still governs whether those statuses gain a code path or are removed. Acceptance authorizes nothing else. Ecosystem M13 stays Proposed on the roadmap with no backlog item, and increment 1 remains unscheduled.

Nineteen user-visible strings rendered "translation missing" in both languages, on four shipped screens, from three separate mistakes. Twelve reader controls - width, font size, theme, export, contents and their aria-labels - were filed under proposal_request rather than academic, so every label on the reader bar of a published academic post was missing while a complete set of translations sat two hundred lines away under the wrong parent. Four more were written yes: and no:, which YAML 1.1 reads as booleans, so the key stopped being the word the file plainly shows and the mentor evaluation's outcomes-met options and the job application's timing line asked for keys that were not there. Two flash keys across three refusal paths were never written at all. SPEC-0005 is accepted and states reader controls carry Thai and English labels; it had been false since the increment shipped. What is worth keeping is why none of it was caught. The parity gate added the same week compares English to Thai, and both files were identically wrong, so it passed - parity is agreement, not correctness. The system test renders that screen and asserts nothing about the control bar. And raise_on_missing_translations was commented out, which is the only check that reads what a screen actually resolved rather than what the file appears to say. The neighbouring paid: true/false keys were quoted too. They resolve today by accident of how I18n normalises a path segment, and depending on that is how the yes/no pair was written in the first place.

Close the class rather than the instance. Two checks join locale parity and one flag is turned on. The first reads every key the code names literally - 1135 of them across app/ and lib/ - and fails on any that is defined nowhere, naming the file and line rather than the key alone; run against the tree before DEV-016 it reports all twenty references by name. The second fails on any locale key that is not a String after YAML parses it, which is five lines and the only thing that makes the yes:/no: trap visible, since the file reads correctly and the lookup is what is wrong; it names twelve keys on the old tree. Neither can see an interpolated key, and there are 177 of those, so raise_on_missing_translations is on in the test environment for the half that is only observable at render time. Turning it on immediately found a twentieth string neither static check could reach: enrollment validates that a section holds students and adds :not_student, a message defined in neither locale, so an administrator who tried to enrol a staff account was refused in words the reader could not read. That is the argument for the flag in one example - the static check reads what the code asks for by name, and this key is never named by the code at all. A green run over files that already agree proves nothing, so both checks were run against the pre-fix tree first and each fired with the offending keys spelled out.

ADR-0049 decision 7 says no proposal writes to docs/ or docs/backlog.json automatically, because the backlog is the source of truth for delivery and its updates carry recorded human approval - a queue that can append to it is a queue that can approve work. The ADR's own fitness function said the decision is enforced by the absence of any write path from application code, which no test asserts today. This is that test, written for the class rather than for proposals: nothing under app/ or lib/ writes a file at all, which is stronger than any per-feature check and needs no revisiting when the triage screen arrives. Two writers are named with the sentence saying what each writes, in the shape the route reachability list already uses, and a second test fails when a named writer stops writing so the list cannot quietly become fiction. The carve-out found while reading the code is that one generated file does live under docs/: lib/error_pages.rb writes the hosted 503 that Render's maintenance mode serves from the documentation origin, and the test pins it to exactly that path and asserts every other generated page belongs in public/. A fourth check states the point in the ADR's own terms - no specification, decision, runbook, or the backlog itself is inside the set of files any code generates. Three injections confirmed it fails: a File.write to the backlog from a service was named with its file and line, the generator repointed at docs/backlog.json failed two checks at once, and a writer that writes nothing was reported as stale. Note what this does not do - script/ writes the dashboard and is deliberately out of scope, because it is tooling a person runs rather than something a request can reach.

M13's stated outcome is the proportion of proposals receiving an auditable decision and an author-visible explanation, and that proportion was zero by construction: nothing assigned status, no screen existed on which anybody could answer a proposal, and the author's page rendered a status that could never move. The user answered the two questions ADR-0049 left open and increment 1 shipped against them. The triage screen is a Proposals tab in the admin console rather than the existing Approvals queue - reuse looked cheaper than it is, because approval_requests requires a course, its decisions require an administrator by a rule written for course lifecycle, and its outcomes are approved and rejected, which a triage outcome is not - and rather than the instructor workspace, because user_must_be_a_contributor admits instructors as authors, so instructors would be deciding proposals they may themselves submit. The status vocabulary stays at the four already shipped and all four become reachable, which turned the migration decision 6 anticipated into no migration of proposal_requests at all: the check constraint and STATUSES already listed exactly these four, and the defect was that three had no code path. A decision is a row, not a column - actor, time, the status it moved to, and the reason - written in the same transaction as the status under a row lock, so a status without the record explaining it cannot exist and two administrators deciding at once produce one decision and one refusal. planned and declined are terminal, because an author must not be told two contradictory things about one submission. There is exactly one reason field and no internal note, since a second one immediately raises the field-visibility question §15 has not answered. The author is told on the page they already have, at their next visit, which is ADR-0049 decision 4 standing while ADR-0004 defers production email; telling them through the bell would have been small and was deliberately not done, because notifications are §15 decision 9 and unanswered. Deciding is audited at warn level naming the reference and the outcome and never the reason, which is the author's words back to them rather than an audit concern. The assertion SPEC-0049 said could not be written until decision 6 was settled is now the last test in the model file: every status the constraint allows is reached for real, one at a time, and no other status is. No public surface was opened and none is authorized - the roadmap section says so in the same paragraph that records what shipped.

Twenty-five list screens loaded every row they could see, and the per-screen query budget could not see it: the budget counts queries, not rows, so every one of them was constant-cost while the result set, the HTML and the transfer grew with the institution. One list had a bound and its bound was worse than none - the audit tab took AuditEvent::RECENT, the most recent fifty after the level filter, and no route reached the rest, on a log the model says cannot be cleared. The user chose paging over a frontend library, and ADR-0050 settled the rest: one Page object of about forty lines rather than Kaminari or Pagy, whose view helpers would have been fought back into the token system the way ADR-0007 refused Tiptap-s styling; ?page= beside the tab, role, q, level and search params, so a page is linkable, survives the back button and needs no JavaScript; twenty-five rows in one constant; an impossible page clamping to the nearest real one, which is the whitelist-or-default rule tab_for and role_filter already run; and a filter change landing on page 1 while a page link keeps the filter. The consequence paragraph predicted seven screens and the enumeration produced nine - the approval queue, which is every course-lifecycle request ever raised, and the public job search, which is the most-read list in the application - both inside controllers the decision already named, and both corrected in the ADR rather than rounded to. The queue came out one query cheaper than it went in, because its template asked AdminConsole.queue twice, once to test for empty and once to render. Every other list is named in SPEC-0051 as either bounded by construction - a cohort, a term, a company-s staff - or growing and deferred, which is the honest half of decision 8: the internship queues, the programs, the placements, the organization index and the notification bell grow with the institution, are outside the decision-s touches, and are UX-009 rather than an omission nobody wrote down.

Increment 1 paged the nine lists inside ADR-0050-s touches and named six more that grow and were not reached. Five of them page now: a company-s incoming internship requests, the published programmes and a company-s own, a programme-s applicants, the placements screen, and the organization index - fifteen screens and seventeen lists in total, and SPEC-0051-s table is the register of both increments. Nothing new was decided; the rule was always lists that grow with the institution, and these are in four controllers the decision did not happen to name. The placements screen forced the one rule increment 1 had no need of. It holds three lists that grow - what a company hosts, what an account supervises, and for an administrator every placement there is - and a single ?page= would have moved all three at once, so a reader paging into the hosting list would have found the supervising one had jumped too. Page now carries the name of the param it owns, page_url replaces that one and carries every other param through including the other lists- pages, and the three are hosting_page, supervising_page and administering_page. The student-s own placements stay a relation rather than a page: they are bounded by a degree, and a control on a list of two is the noise decision 8 refused. What is left is the notification bell, and it is left deliberately. It is capped at eight with no route to the ninth, which is the audit log-s defect in miniature, but the fix is a screen rather than a page - a dropdown in the header has nowhere to put a control, and a notification history needs a route, a place in the navigation and a rule about what a read notification does. That is a new surface and therefore an ADR, so the cap stays and both the decision and the specification now say why rather than leaving it to be rediscovered.

Three roadmap tables disagreed with the backlog and with each other. The AI recruitment track called all fifteen of its milestones Proposed while every one of them had a complete backlog item behind an accepted specification and ADR; the ecosystem track called M11 increments 1 to 3 after increment 4 shipped, and M13 Proposed after increment 1 delivered the same morning. DEV-005 built a gate for exactly this and it caught none of them, because it only reads the consolidated table, the UTCC summary table and the UTCC section status lines - the two track tables are outside it. The deeper problem was the gate-s rule rather than its reach. It held that a milestone whose backlog items are all complete must say Complete, and six AI milestones have one complete item each whose specification calls the shipped increment narrower than the milestone: an advisory next-action panel rather than a recruiter agent, preparation prompts rather than a candidate or internship agent, one organization-scoped workflow report rather than analytics, an in-app conversation rather than notifications, and a reviewable control contract rather than an integration. The rule therefore demanded the word Complete against outcome text describing capabilities nobody built, and the consolidated table duly said it. First slice is now the second delivered label, meaning the tracked work is finished and the milestone-s own description is larger - the only part a file can testify to is item status, and scope is a human judgement. Both directions of the original check survive: a milestone with open items may claim neither label, and a milestone with none open must claim one. Ecosystem M13 is now mapped and checked, which it never was, and test/scripts/validate_backlog_roadmap_test.rb is the gate on the gate, including that a word merely starting like the label does not pass for it. The outcome columns keep the destination rather than being rewritten to what shipped, because the ordering exists to describe where the platform is going; the Status cell carries what exists, and a new table under the AI roadmap names for each of the six what shipped, what did not, and which specification says so.

The user asked for Vue to be available to the frontend for some code, was shown the constraints, and reaffirmed. The coding standard admits a JavaScript package only behind an accepted ADR naming the capability, the alternatives including no dependency, maintenance and security ownership, failure and removal paths, and the licence position, so ADR-0051 and SPEC-0052 are what the library arrived with. Three facts about this application decided its shape. The CSP is script-src self with a nonce and no unsafe-eval, and bin/importmap pin vue fetches the full build, which compiles templates with Function() - blocked in production, silently, on a screen that passes every test that never loaded the header. So the runtime-only build is vendored instead, islands render with h rather than templates, and test/operations/vue_build_test.rb asserts the vendored bytes carry no compiler, because re-running the pin command after an upgrade is exactly how this regresses. There is no JavaScript build step, so single-file components are not available and adding a bundler was refused as a larger decision than this one. Turbo replaces the body on navigation and any node on a stream, so createApp is called in exactly one file - a Stimulus bridge whose connect and disconnect Turbo already drives - and that is asserted too. An island is named through a registry rather than imported by markup, which is the whitelist-or-default rule the console params already run on; its copy arrives as props already translated, so the bilingual invariant keeps one home; and it enhances markup that works without it, so a failed mount costs the enhancement and not the screen. Alpine was rejected for needing unsafe-eval, React and Preact on weak evidence that would be the first to revisit, and plain Stimulus stays the default for everything not state-shaped - the seventeen existing controllers are not rewritten. The first island is the character counter on the proposal decision reason, the text an author reads under a thousand-character limit: small, reversible, and it exercises the whole path from pin to both locales. What a browser proves is not covered here - islands are visible only to system tests - so the server-side half is asserted instead: the island names a field that exists on the page, its limit equals the maxlength that field enforces, and its template still carries the interpolation the island fills.

DEV-019 corrected three roadmap tables by hand and left two of them outside the gate, which is how they drifted in the first place: the check read the consolidated table, the UTCC summary table and the UTCC section status lines, and neither track table. It reads all five now. The obstacle was that a track table names a bare M10 and there are three different M10s in the file, so the enclosing section heading is tracked and the bare ID resolved through it - AI Recruitment Platform Roadmap to AI-M10, Company Business Case Platform Roadmap to M10-CBP, M11-SIR and M13. A row under a section with no mapping is nobody-s milestone and is left alone rather than guessed at. One bug fell out of turning it on: status is the fourth column in a track table and the last in the two planning tables, so reading the last cell in all three reported every AI row as saying whatever its dependency column held, which is why the first run complained that AI-M8 says M6, M7. Both facts are now asserted in the gate-s own test. Turning the check on also forced two ecosystem rows into the two-label vocabulary. M10 is First slice - phase 1 is invitation-only and text-only, and uploads, email and reporting remain proposals. M11 is Complete, because its own section says every authorized increment of SPEC-0041 has shipped and the remainder - interviews, an academic gate, rubric evaluation, email, REST APIs, academic credit - is unauthorized rather than pending, and is enforced absent by a boundary test.

UX-010 shipped the first Vue island with its server-side half asserted and its browser half not, and said so in both documents: the island names a field that exists with the limit that field enforces and the copy from both locale files, none of which proves it mounts. Three failures are visible nowhere else - a CSP that blocks the build, which is exactly what the full Vue build would have done and what the vendored-bytes test exists to prevent; a bridge or registry that never mounts; and an island bound to the wrong field, which counts nothing while looking correct. The walk covers all three: the counter reads a thousand on an empty field, counts down as an administrator types, changes tone within a hundred of the limit, and the decision still records with the island on the page - which is the enhancement rule from the other side, since the form owes the island nothing. The full system suite was run first and passed at 28, then at 30 with these two. The spec and the decision no longer carry this as an open item.

ADR-0052 is proposed and not accepted, and no work is authorized by it. Notification::RECENT is eight and no route reaches the ninth, which is the defect ADR-0050 took out of the audit log with one difference that matters: the audit log is a screen and the bell is a dropdown in the header, so a pagination control inside a menu that closes on outside-click is worse than the cap. The fix is a screen, which is a new surface and therefore a decision. It matters more than the row count suggests because ADR-0004 defers production email, so the bell is the only channel there is - a student invited to a business case, a company told a request arrived, a supervisor assigned to a placement each learn about it there or not at all, and eight is one busy week. Five questions carry recommendations and need a human answer: whether the reader-facing URL takes /notifications while the bell-s frame endpoint moves under it, whether read rows stay so the screen answers what was I told rather than what is waiting, whether opening the screen marks everything read - recommended no, because a dot that clears by being looked at means you have not visited rather than something happened, whether the bell keeps its eight and gains a link, and whether a notification can be deleted. The last has a real counter-argument recorded with it: these are personal rows rather than an institutional record, and a screen built on nothing is deleted differs from one built on the reader owns their list in more than a button. Doing nothing is listed as an alternative and is defensible today, which is why this is proposed rather than assumed.

The user answered ADR-0052 by taking all five recommendations as written, so the decision is accepted and SPEC-0053 records what shipped. /notifications is the reader-s own history now - every row ever written for them, newest first, paged at twenty-five like every other list that grows - and the bell-s frame endpoint moved to /notifications/bell, because the readable URL belongs to the reader-s screen and the frame is an implementation detail of the header. It is a history rather than an inbox: read rows stay, since an inbox that empties as you read it answers what is waiting, which the dot already answers, and the question this screen exists for is what was I told. Reading the screen marks nothing read - a dot that clears by being looked at means you have not visited rather than something happened, and would dismiss the seven the reader did not come for - so the one write stays the explicit button, which the screen carries a copy of when something is unread. The bell keeps its eight and gains see all at the foot of the panel, which is the route the ninth row was missing, and there is no navigation entry because the bell is where a reader already goes to ask this. Nothing is deleted and nothing prunes, matching AuditEvent, with the counter-argument recorded rather than dismissed. Two predictions in the decision were corrected against what shipped: notifications#show stops being a route-reachability exception because it is the page now, but notifications#bell takes its place, so the exception moved rather than disappeared; and the bell and the screen do not share a partial - they share the model, which is what actually keeps the sentence, the action link and the read state from drifting, while a dropdown row and a card differ in markup by design. This is the sixteenth paged screen and the last list SPEC-0051 named as growing without a bound.

ADR-0051 took Vue with no build step and paid for it in one place: the CSP is script-src self with no unsafe-eval, which blocks Vue-s template compiler, so an island had to be a hand-written h() render function - recorded at the time as the reason a bundler would be the next decision if single-file components turned out to matter. The user asked for Vite after being shown what it costs, and it resolves the problem without touching the policy, because the compiler moves to the toolchain: a .vue file is compiled at build time and the browser receives render code and the runtime alone. Vite builds the island layer and nothing else. app/javascript stays the import map-s - Turbo, Stimulus, seventeen controllers, sixty Tiptap pins - and app/frontend is Vite-s, with neither importing from the other, because a shared module would ship twice. Vue left the import map and the vendored runtime build was deleted, since two toolchains carrying Vue is two Vues. The counter island was rewritten as a single-file component with the same behavior, which is the proof the path works. The bridge moved with it: Stimulus cannot host it any more because its bundle cannot import Vite-s, so the entrypoint owns the lifecycle with a MutationObserver plus a turbo:before-cache unmount, which covers what Stimulus covered - Drive replacing the body, and a Stream replacing one node with no page event at all. createApp still has exactly one caller and an island is still a name in a registry rather than an import. The CSP is unchanged in production and test and weaker in development only, where the HMR client needs unsafe_eval and its own origin; it is a conditional in the policy rather than a comment, so it cannot silently apply elsewhere. Node is a build dependency and never a runtime one: the Dockerfile installs a pinned version in the build stage, runs npm ci and precompile, and deletes node_modules before the final image. npm audit joins bundler-audit and importmap audit in the security gate, because a Vite dependency tree was the third supply chain and nothing watched it. The bundle is 61KB against 110KB vendored, tree-shaken. Inertia was rejected and written down as rejected: it replaces the view layer, does not coexist with Turbo, moves copy out of the locale files and leaves a screen blank without JavaScript, so it would be a rewrite with its own ADR rather than an extension of this one.

bin/dev has been unusable outside an interactive shell, and it took two failures today to see it rather than one. Tailwind-s watcher exits immediately when stdout is not a terminal, and foreman stops the whole group the moment any process exits, so the symptom is the server booting and dying two seconds later with no error of its own - which reads as a port problem or a crash, not as a watcher that declined to watch. The gem-s own answer is the always argument, so Procfile.dev now runs tailwindcss:watch[always] with a comment saying why. All three processes stay up, including the Vite dev server, and the page carries the client tag and the entrypoint from localhost:3036 with a nonce, under the development-only CSP relaxation ADR-0053 describes and nothing wider. The second failure in the same sequence was a stale tmp/pids/server.pid left by a killed server, which is worth remembering as the other reason web exits at once. The production image was then built and inspected, which is the step the Vite commit said it could not run. All four properties hold: the island bundle and its manifest are present under public/vite, node_modules is absent, node and npm are not on the PATH, and /usr/local/node - where the build stage installs it - does not exist in the final stage. Node is a build dependency and nothing in the running image can execute it.

The bridge moved from Stimulus to a MutationObserver when Vite arrived, and the path that replaced Stimulus-s connect had no test: an island mounted on first load and nothing proved it mounted again after Turbo replaced or restored the DOM. The walk now navigates away through Turbo Drive, comes back, and asserts one counter - not two, not none - that is still live rather than a leftover string, by typing into the field and watching the number move. Both halves of the bridge were then mutated to see what the test is worth. Deleting the observer-s mount of added nodes fails it: the restored page has an empty div. Deleting the turbo:before-cache unmount does not fail it, because Turbo clones the snapshot and the observer mounts a fresh app over whatever it held - so the comment claiming that failure was corrected rather than left standing. The unmount is defensive and stays: it keeps Vue-s output out of the cached HTML, so what a reader sees during the restore flash is the server-s markup rather than a stale render. That is written down as what this test is not evidence for. The same observer path is what a Turbo Stream takes when it replaces a node, which is still undriven by any test and is named as such.

config/ci.rb gained two steps today and had never been run end to end, so it was - and it caught two things, one of them mine. Brakeman was failing the gate and had been since 8.0.6 shipped: bin/brakeman prepends --ensure-latest, so a release anybody makes turns the step red without a line of this repository changing. It was reported as passing several times during the day because the command was read through a pipe, which returns grep-s exit status and not Brakeman-s; the scan itself found nothing then and finds nothing now, but the step was red and was called green. The gem is bumped and the reading corrected. The second was a race introduced with Vite. autoBuild builds the island bundle on the first request for an asset, which in a parallel suite is eight processes discovering a stale bundle at the same moment - several build at once and one reads public/vite-test while another is part-way through rewriting it. The symptom is a template error saying the entrypoint is not in the manifests, on whichever few tests rendered a layout inside the window, which reads exactly like a flake. It is not one: it passed on the first gate run and failed on the next two, and passed every standalone run because the bundle was already warm. autoBuild is off in test now and test_helper builds once in the parent process before parallelize forks, so every worker inherits a manifest that is already correct. Verified from a cold start with public/vite-test deleted, and the whole gate is green in 1m18s: setup, docs, RuboCop, three audits, Brakeman, the Vite build, 1318 unit tests, the seed replant, and 31 system tests.

A comment in the lesson view said KaTeX was unavailable because the app vendored no CSS or fonts, and offered the monospace branch as the fallback it expects. Both halves were stale. katex.js, katex.css and twenty font files have been vendored since the academic-post editor took Tiptap, the stylesheet is in shared/_head, and the editor typesets with them - so math was already rendered in this application, in the one place authors write LaTeX. The first reading of this was wrong in the other direction: the twelve real topics carry prose formulas, not LaTeX, and running a typesetter over input + model to output to evaluation would italicise every word and choke on the arrows, so monospace is the right rendering for them. The guard written to hold that line failed on its first run and found the actual defect. The generic placeholder copy, which the three topics outside REAL_TOPIC_KEYS fall back to, is genuine LaTeX - n_{train} = \lceil 0.8\,N \rceil, \quad n_{test} = N - n_{train} - in both locales, and every learner reaching 5-2, 6-1 or 6-2 was shown that string as monospace source. Block#latex? now decides per block: a backslash command or a $ pair means maths and gets a Stimulus controller that calls katex.render, anything else is printed as written. Subscript braces alone are deliberately not enough, because w_{new} = w_{old} - learning rate is a sentence. Stimulus rather than a Vue island, since this is behavior attached to server-rendered markup and holds no state - ADR-0051 decision 7. The source is in the markup either way, so a reader without JavaScript sees the expression rather than an empty plate. Three tests: the split asserted from both sides in both locales, the server handing the controller only to the LaTeX block, and a browser walk proving it is typeset rather than merely wrapped, with MathML present for a screen reader. The walk was mutation-checked - stub the render call and it fails.

The KaTeX defect hid behind a comment claiming a limitation that had stopped being true, so the same class was swept for rather than the instance being called done. Numeric claims are the checkable part of it, and every one checked was wrong. The style policy said nineteen inline style attributes across ten templates; there are thirty across fifteen. Three documents and CLAUDE.md said seventeen Stimulus controllers; there are thirteen, and the number was probably absorbed from Organization#from_param!, whose own seventeen is correct - seventeen Rails controllers really do look an organization up. ADR-0053 said sixty pins where there are sixty-three, and carried a consequence that autoBuild covers test, which the race fix had already made false the same night. The substance under the count matters more than the count. unsafe-inline is in style-src because every inline style is a value Ruby worked out - a progress width, a stagger delay, a toast offset, one background-image URL - and a utility class cannot express those. That was true of twenty-nine of the thirty. The thirtieth was style=animation-delay: 60ms on the catalogue subtitle, which a utility could express and which nothing would have noticed a second or a tenth of. It is [animation-delay:60ms] now, and inline_style_boundary_test.rb holds the rule from both sides: an inline style must carry a computed value, and the computed ones must still be there - so the policy cannot be satisfied by quietly deleting the feature it exists for.

The Vite build shipped a source map to production - 535KB beside a 61KB bundle, served publicly, holding the island sources - on the argument that a bundle nobody can read cannot be reviewed after an incident. It was flagged when it went in and left for a decision; the decision is that the argument needs somewhere for the map to go and there is nowhere. Nothing in this application consumes source maps: no error tracker, no upload step, and no other bundle ships one, because Propshaft serves the import map-s files as they were written. It would have been the only map in production, nine times the size of what it explains, and the only thing reading it would have been whoever wanted the sources. Off in production, on in every other mode, verified by running a production assets:precompile and finding the bundle alone. If an error tracker ever arrives the answer is to upload the map to it rather than serve it from the origin, and the ADR says so. The rule is asserted against the configuration rather than a production build, in the same shape as the importmap assertion beside it, because the suite builds in test mode where the map is deliberately present.

docs/performance.md said its table was measured per render against the seeds, and one of the last edits to it - mine, earlier the same night - was made by reasoning about a change rather than by rendering anything. Measuring it found the table wrong by two to three times across the board: catalog said 13 and measures 33, admin said 12 to 20 and measures 23 to 59. It had drifted through several increments that each added a query or four, and nobody had rendered a screen to check. script/measure-screens is the reproduction, so the next correction is a command rather than an argument, and it carries the warning that replanting the seeds into the test database leaves rows the fixtures cannot clear - the next bin/rails test fails with foreign key violations that look nothing like their cause. The script found a live defect before its numbers were used. The company work surface raised Translation missing for recruitment.company_work.queues.active_placements_note. Every queue in the waiting grid renders a note; active_placements has none, in either locale, because whoever wrote the copy wrote notes for the two real queues and stopped. It only appears there when the count is non-zero, so a company hosting a running internship met a missing translation on its own front door while every test ran against a company that had none - and locale parity could not see it, since the key is missing from both files and is interpolated rather than literal. A running placement is not work waiting on anybody and already has its own card under what is running, so Queue carries a waiting flag now and the grid selects on it. The regression test renders the surface with an active placement in both locales and was mutation-checked: restore the old select and it fails with the same missing key. Two figures are recorded as open questions rather than fixed: admin features at 59 reads like a query per flag, and admin users at 36 is high for a paged list.

DEV-027 recorded two figures as open questions rather than fixing them, and both had an answer. The feature-control tab ran 59 queries and 46 were the same single-row find_by on feature_settings: nearly every screen asks whether a flag is on - the header, the footer, the nav, the bell, two admin tabs - and each ask went to the database, while admin_rows asked once per key inside a loop that ran once per flag. Three rows are read once on Current now, the same bargain as the syllabus and the landing copy and held there for the same reason, that a module-level memo outlives the database it was read from when the parallel runner forks. The tab is 14 and every other screen came down with it: the catalogue lost two, the overview nine, the roster the rest. Invalidation is a model callback rather than the writer remembering, because the first test to fail was one that wrote a row directly instead of through the approved class method - a console session would do the same. The roster ran 36 queries with one membership existence check per row, because .active on an association builds a fresh relation and returns to the database however loaded the rows already are. company_member? folds in Ruby now and the roster preloads, so a full page of twenty-five asks once for everybody; the screen is 18. Both are held by query_budget_test.rb and both tests were checked by putting the old code back. The measured table in performance.md is updated from the same script.

The measurement script could not open a company-s internship request queue as an administrator, which turned out to be correct and to point at something that was not. SPEC-0041-s access matrix gives an administrator a placement record to assign or revoke a supervisor and nothing wider - no unbounded browsing of student documents - so the queue answering 404 is the specified behaviour. ADR-0048 decision 4 puts the whole board in front of every active member, deliberately, because a mentor who cannot decide a request is still better off knowing a student has been waiting since Tuesday. Both rules are right. What was wrong was the link between them: a mentor and an administrator each saw a card on the work surface linking to a queue that answered them 404, on a screen they are meant to be on, and mentor is a member role that is not a decider. The count stays and the link goes, for exactly the readers who are refused - Queue#openable? is whether this viewer may open where the card points, and the card renders as a plain div when they cannot. It costs one membership check, which the query budget caught immediately as 13 becoming 14; the ceiling moved by exactly that with the reason recorded, and the assertion still names the per-status regression it is really watching for. SPEC-0048 invariant 5 said every figure is a count with a link to the queue it counts, which is no longer true and should not be; it now carries the qualifier and the reason two rules meet there. ADR-0048 records the correction in its consequences.

route_reachability_test holds one half of every route leads somewhere - the action exists, and a GET that renders no template says why. The reader-s half was unheld: a screen may link to a place the person looking at it is refused, which is how the work surface came to hand a mentor and an administrator a link to a 404. script/crawl-links follows every rendered anchor as each of the four readers, GET only because a button_to is a form and following those would decide proposals on the way past. It found two more, both live. New internship programme raised a 500 for everybody allowed to open it, from the day it shipped: the form said form_with model: [ organization, program ], which asks Rails for organization_recruitment_internship_programs_path while the routes are named company_. Every test posted straight to the create action, so nothing had ever rendered the screen a person has to use to get there. It takes form_url and form_method now, the way its sibling job-post form already did. And six of the eight courses offered a syllabus download that answers 404 - they carry no module rows, so the PDF correctly refuses, and the syllabus a learner reads on those pages is the default taxonomy standing in until a real curriculum lands. Course#syllabus? decides, one query, only on the page that uses it. Both tests were checked by putting the old code back. All four readers now crawl clean: 280, 132, 154 and 139 pages, every link leading somewhere.

script/crawl-links exits non-zero when a link leads somewhere its reader cannot go, and says how many pages it stopped short of rather than implying it cleared them. The first run after it became a gate passed with every reader crawling nine public pages: the seeds had been replaced by fixtures, all four sign-ins failed silently, and every link led somewhere was true and worthless. A gate that cannot tell clean from never got in is worse than no gate, so each reader now proves it is signed in by opening a page only an authenticated one gets, and the script aborts naming the reader and telling you to replant the seeds. Verified both ways: exit 1 without seeds, exit 0 with them.

The teaching dashboard was one screen and three routes - a roster, a grades CSV, a proctoring switch - and every course control lived behind allow_only :admin. The user asked for a teacher who can create, update, enable, disable and approve certificates, then asked for recommendations on the four questions that scope it, and took all four. Two of the four are refusals with their blockers named. A course-s words are catalog.courses.code in two locale files and the table carries identity, taxonomy and numbers only, so a course created through a form would render translation missing on every screen naming it; moving that copy into the database is its own decision with LandingText as the precedent. And ADR-0011 deferred certificate issuance - no artifact, no rule, no identity, no route - so an approval button would approve nothing while looking like it certified somebody. What shipped is the other two. A teacher edits the numbers of the course their section teaches while it is unpublished: level, credits, projects, hours, core, certificate. Not the code, which every locale key and completion row is joined by; not the lifecycle state, which belongs to the queue; not learners or rating, which are measured rather than set - and a form made to post them changes none of them. Enable and disable are the existing lifecycle rather than a second switch that would answer can a learner see this twice. A transition is requested, never made: ApprovalRequest widened by exactly one rule, that a requester may be an approver or the course-s teacher, and approvable_by? is untouched, so a teacher cannot decide their own request and neither can the administrator who raised one. That refusal is what ADR-0013 bought and it was checked by removing the new rule, which fails the test. An administrator holds the staff role, teaches nothing, and is offered no course panel; their authority stays the console.
